chapter_title: A Bottle of Dew (Fables and Folk Tales)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading and Unpacking the Folk Tale

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — Part I (p.3): Rama Natha's belief and the sage's advice.
Let us discuss — Part II (p.5): why Rama Natha was angry and how wealth was created.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the folk tale aloud (pp. 1–5) with students following in their books. Pause briefly after each part to let students absorb the scene.
Using "Let us discuss" after Part I (p.3), the class explores what Rama Natha believed and how the sage responded. Students share answers in pairs before a brief whole-class check.
Using "Let us discuss" after Part II (p.5), students discuss why Rama Natha felt angry and trace how he and Madhumati together built their wealth. Teacher draws out key ideas on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The folk tale rewards a unhurried reading aloud — Rama Natha's gullibility and the sage's quiet wisdom are best felt at the pace of the storytelling. A common pitfall is jumping to the moral before students have noticed that Madhumati's enterprise at the market is equal to Rama Natha's labour in the fields. The task on creating wealth (p.5) is a good prompt to surface that partnership. Students curious about the sage's precise instructions may explore pp. 2–3 on their own.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on the Story and Listening to Madhumati

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect I (p.6–7): True/False statements and MCQ on event sequence.
Let us listen (p.10): number Madhumati's actions in the order they happen.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II (p.7): answer the five questions about the sage's plan and the banana plantation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a comprehension-discussion on "Let us think and reflect I" (pp. 6–7), focusing on the True/False statements about Madhumati and Rama Natha, and on the MCQ sequencing the key events at the sage's hut. Students write answers individually, then compare with a partner.
Teacher reads the listening transcript (p.36) aloud at a measured pace while students follow the event list in "Let us listen" (p.10) and number each action in the correct order.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students check and correct their numbering. A quick whole-class comparison surfaces any events that were tricky to sequence.

periods.teacher_notes: The True/False task on Madhumati's feelings (p.6) often trips students who conflate her worry with unhappiness — keep the discussion grounded in what the prose actually says. For the listening sequence, remind students to hold their pen and listen fully on the first reading before writing, mirroring real-world listening behaviour. The five questions in "Let us think and reflect II" (p.7) work well as independent reading homework to consolidate the story arc.

periods.activity_title: Speaking on Hard Work and Exploring Homophones

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.11): paired discussion on what hard work means and why it matters.
Let us learn (p.8): match Column A story words with their homophones in Column B.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly models how to use the sentence starters in "Let us speak" (p.11) — "It means… / Firstly, I feel… / To begin with…" — so students hear the register before they use it.

Students work in pairs on the three guided-conversation questions (p.11): what hard work means to them, three reasons it matters, and three pieces of advice for someone who needs to work harder. Teacher circulates, prompting quieter students with the hint phrases.
Two or three pairs share their ideas with the class; teacher notes a selection of reasons and advice on the board to build a shared word bank.

Students turn to the homophones table (p.8) under "Let us learn." Teacher introduces the concept of homophones using the story-word pairs (dew/due, son/sun, ate/eight, see/sea), and students complete the meanings of the Column B words in pairs.

periods.teacher_notes: The guided-conversation task benefits from the teacher briefly modelling a complete response before pairs begin — this lowers the threshold for students who are uncertain about speaking at length. In the homophones table, students sometimes confuse "due" (scheduled) with "dew" (moisture) because both appear in the story; grounding each meaning in a sentence from real life helps. The tongue-twister task (p.9) is a lively extension students may explore voluntarily.

periods.activity_title: Connecting Words and Sentences in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.8): fill the paragraph blanks with the correct story words.
Let us learn (p.9): match phrases using connecting words (because, before, as soon as, as).

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.9): write four sentences each using one pair of homophones from the table.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the fill-in paragraph (p.8) using the eight story words (promised, spending, cheated, luck, remember, huge, difficult, market) individually. Teacher then works through the answers with the class, asking students to explain why each word fits.

Teacher introduces the four connecting words (because, before, as soon as, as) and their functions in a sentence. Students match the phrase pairs (p.9) and write the completed sentences in their notebooks; teacher circulates to check that the connecting word chosen creates a logical meaning.
Pairs compare sentences aloud for two or three items; teacher highlights where different connecting words would change the meaning, reinforcing the concept.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently choose 'because' for every blank in the matching task without reading both halves of the sentence — prompt them to check what kind of link is needed (reason, time, or comparison) before selecting. The fill-in paragraph (p.8) contains two extra words; remind students to read the whole paragraph once before filling any blank. The homophone sentence-writing task (p.9) travels well as homework since it consolidates what was explored in the previous sitting on the dew/due word family.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Bananas and Exploring India's Varieties

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.11–12): write eight sentences describing a banana using the word-map clues.
Let us explore (p.12): discuss and begin noting varieties of bananas grown across India.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads through the word-map clues on p.11–12 with the class — smell, taste, colour, texture of the peel, when to eat, health benefits — so every student has a clear picture of what to cover.

Working in pairs, students draft eight sentences describing a banana, drawing on the word-map clues. Teacher circulates, encouraging precise descriptive language and full sentences. Pairs share two or three sentences aloud; teacher offers brief oral feedback on clarity and detail.

Teacher introduces the "Let us explore" task (p.12): the story's banana plantation opens a question about the many varieties grown across India. Small groups quickly brainstorm varieties they know (by name, appearance, or region) and note them down — this seeds the research they can deepen independently.
Groups share one or two varieties each; teacher lists them on the board, noting the regions named. Students are pointed to the NHB website (p.12) as a resource for their own further reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The banana description task works best when students are encouraged to use sensory detail — the feel of a ripe peel, the sweetness of the flesh — rather than only factual statements. A common gap is neglecting to mention health benefits or the 'when to eat' dimension from the word map; a quick reminder at the drafting stage helps. For the exploration task, the in-class discussion is productive even when internet access is limited, as students often bring regional knowledge of banana varieties from home.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets events and character motivations using a prose folk tale as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rama Natha's obsession with a magic potion, the sage's ruse, Madhumati's enterprise, six-year banana plantation, wealth revealed.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes why Sage Mahipati asked Rama Natha to collect five litres of morning dew himself, refusing to let anyone else do the work?

options.label: A
options.text: The sage feared that a helper might steal the dew before it could be enchanted.

options.label: B
options.text: The sage knew that the labour of tending banana plants would itself create wealth, and no helper could do that on Rama Natha's behalf.

options.label: C
options.text: The sage wanted Rama Natha to realise that dew water alone holds magical properties.

options.label: D
options.text: The sage was testing whether Rama Natha was strong enough to carry heavy bags of dew.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student misread the sage's ruse as a genuine claim about dew's properties rather than a plan to make Rama Natha work.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a detail about theft that has no basis in the story — the student may be confusing motivation with a plot element not present.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Focuses on physical strength rather than the wisdom-through-labour theme central to the folk tale.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets events and character motivations using a prose folk tale as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rama Natha's obsession with a magic potion, the sage's ruse, Madhumati's enterprise, six-year banana plantation, wealth revealed.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, Madhumati steps forward with a large box of gold coins rather than waiting for Rama Natha to react to the failed magic. What does this moment reveal about Madhumati's role in the couple's success, and how does it change what we understand about who really drove the family's fortune? Write your answer in two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Madhumati's stepping forward with the gold coins reveals that she was an equal partner in building the family's wealth — not a bystander to Rama Natha's labour. While Rama Natha tended the fields and collected dew, it was Madhumati's enterprise in selling the banana crop at the market over six years that converted their hard work into real wealth, showing that the family's fortune was built by both of them together, not by any single person's effort.

items.item_stem: Listen to the account of Madhumati's day with the bananas. Write the number 1 to 7 in the box next to each event below to show the order in which the events happen.
items.visual_stimulus:
Event | Order
Gives two bananas to a hungry boy on the way home | ___
Visits her neighbour and gives them a bunch of bananas | ___
Goes to the market to sell the bananas | ___
Gives twelve bananas to her friend Kalawati | ___
Visits her mother and gives her two dozen bananas | ___
Meets her old friend Kalawati in the market | ___
Decides to go home as most bananas have been sold | ___

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Visits her mother and gives her two dozen bananas. 2. Goes to the market to sell the bananas. 3. Meets her old friend Kalawati in the market. 4. Gives twelve bananas to her friend Kalawati. 5. Decides to go home as most bananas have been sold. 6. Gives two bananas to a hungry boy on the way home. 7. Visits her neighbour and gives them a bunch of bananas.

items.source_lo: Student sequences events accurately by listening carefully to a spoken narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Madhumati's journey distributing bananas — mother, market, friend Kalawati, hungry boy, neighbour — in order.
items.item_stem: After listening to Madhumati's day, answer the following question in one or two sentences: Madhumati encounters two people outside the market — a friend and a stranger. What does her response to each of them tell us about the kind of person she is?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Madhumati gifts a dozen bananas to her friend Kalawati and gives two bananas to a hungry boy she does not know. Her generosity towards both a familiar friend and a complete stranger shows that she is a warm-hearted and compassionate person who shares her good fortune readily with others.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and elaborates personal views on a theme using structured spoken discourse as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Theme of hard work and persistence, linked to Rama Natha and Madhumati's six-year effort; guided speaking with sentence starters.
items.item_stem: Think about Rama Natha's journey from being someone who chased magical shortcuts to becoming a person who worked the land for six years. In two to three sentences spoken to your partner, describe what that change means and connect it to what hard work means in your own life. Use at least one of these starters: 'It means… / It is something… / What I mean is…'

expected_elements: Names a specific change in Rama Natha's behaviour or attitude.
Makes a clear personal connection to the theme of hard work.
Uses at least one of the provided sentence starters fluently.
Speaks in connected sentences, not isolated words or phrases.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and elaborates personal views on a theme using structured spoken discourse as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Theme of hard work and persistence, linked to Rama Natha and Madhumati's six-year effort; guided speaking with sentence starters.
items.item_stem: Imagine a friend tells you: 'Hard work takes too long — it is better to find a quick way to get rich.' Using ideas from Rama Natha and Madhumati's story, respond to your friend in a short spoken turn of about three to four sentences. Give at least two reasons for your view, and use the linking phrases 'Firstly, I feel… because…' and 'Secondly, I think… since…'

expected_elements: Challenges the friend's view with reference to Rama Natha's or Madhumati's experience.
Gives at least two distinct reasons, signposted with 'Firstly' and 'Secondly'.
Sustains a persuasive or reflective register throughout.
Stays within the story's evidence without inventing new plot details.

items.source_lo: Student composes descriptive sentences using word-map clues as a guided writing scaffold as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Describing a banana: smell, taste, texture of peel, colour, health benefits, when to eat — eight sentences.
items.item_stem:
Use the word-map clues below to write six sentences describing a banana. Make sure each sentence is complete and covers a different detail — you may write about its colour, smell, taste, how the peel feels, when you like to eat it, or why it is healthy.

Word-map clues: colour of the outer covering — texture of the peel — smell — taste — when I like to eat a banana — healthy because

expected_elements: Each sentence addresses a different word-map clue without repetition.
Uses precise descriptive language — for example, names the colour or texture exactly.
All six sentences are grammatically complete with a subject and verb.
Writes in a clear, simple descriptive register appropriate for a fact-file style.

items.source_lo: Student composes descriptive sentences using word-map clues as a guided writing scaffold as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Describing a banana: smell, taste, texture of peel, colour, health benefits, when to eat — eight sentences.
items.item_stem: Rama Natha and Madhumati's plantation produced a rich banana harvest every season. Imagine you are writing a short paragraph for a school magazine persuading your classmates to include bananas in their daily diet. Write five to six sentences. Draw on the descriptive details you know about bananas — their appearance, taste, smell, and health benefits — to make your case convincingly.

expected_elements: Opens with a clear persuasive claim or invitation to eat bananas.
Uses at least three sensory or health details to support the argument.
Maintains a friendly, persuasive tone suited to a school magazine.
Closes with a recommendation or call to action.

items.item_stem:
Complete each sentence below by choosing the correct connecting word from the box. Write one word per blank. (because / before / as soon as / as)

1. Rama Natha began cleaning his fields ________ he wanted to collect dew from the banana leaves.
2. ________ Madhumati arrived at the market, she arranged the bananas carefully on her stall.
3. The sage smiled ________ Rama Natha realised that hard work, not magic, had created the family's wealth.
4. ________ Rama Natha tended the plants year after year, the plantation grew larger and larger.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. because  2. Before  3. as soon as  4. As

items.source_lo: Student applies research and inquiry skills to extend a story's real-world context using hands-on exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Varieties of bananas cultivated and eaten across different regions of India; NHB website as a starting resource.
items.item_stem: Rama Natha and Madhumati built a large banana plantation over six years. India is one of the world's largest banana-growing countries, with many different varieties cultivated across its regions. Using information you have gathered from books, conversations with family members, or the NHB website, list any four varieties of bananas grown in India. For each variety, write the name of the region or state where it is commonly grown and one feature that makes it different from the others (such as its size, colour, taste, or use).

expected_elements: Names at least four distinct banana varieties found in India.
Links each variety to a specific region or state.
Describes one distinguishing feature per variety clearly.
Uses information from an identifiable source, not guesswork.

items.source_lo: Student applies research and inquiry skills to extend a story's real-world context using hands-on exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Varieties of bananas cultivated and eaten across different regions of India; NHB website as a starting resource.
items.item_stem: Design a one-page 'Banana Map of India' project. On an outline map of India, mark at least five states or regions and label one banana variety grown in each. Add a short key at the side that gives the name of each variety and one sentence about its special quality or common use. You may use colour, simple drawings, or symbols to make the map easy to read. Share your completed map with the class and explain two things you found surprising or interesting during your research.

expected_elements: Map marks at least five states or regions accurately.
Each marked region is linked to a correctly named banana variety.
Key entries include one clear, accurate quality or use per variety.
Verbal sharing identifies two genuinely researched surprising findings.
